issues.summary: A1 - Log in and start a role-scoped session
acceptanceCriteria: A user with valid credentials is authenticated and a session is created that carries their role (Event Organiser, Event Coordinator, Venue Staff, Technical Support Staff, or Attendee).
An incorrect email or an incorrect password is rejected with the same message ("email or password is incorrect") so the message does not reveal which field was wrong.
A rejection caused by a deactivated account is distinguishable from a rejection caused by wrong credentials.
On a failed login attempt no session is created and no last-login timestamp is recorded.
On successful login the last-login timestamp and the authenticated user are recorded.
Logging out ends the session; navigating back to a protected page afterwards does not display any event data.
issues.description:
Ref/ID: A1  
Component/Category: User Authentication & Authorisation

**Goal:** Log in and start a session scoped to the user’s role.

**User Story:** As a ConnectSphere User, I want to log in and start a session scoped to my role, so that I can access features permitted for my role.

**Acceptance Criteria:**

* A user with valid credentials is authenticated and a session is created that carries their role (Event Organiser, Event Coordinator, Venue Staff, Technical Support Staff, or Attendee).
* An incorrect email or an incorrect password is rejected with the same message ("email or password is incorrect") so the message does not reveal which field was wrong.
* A rejection caused by a deactivated account is distinguishable from a rejection caused by wrong credentials.
* On a failed login attempt no session is created and no last-login timestamp is recorded.
* On successful login the last-login timestamp and the authenticated user are recorded.
* Logging out ends the session; navigating back to a protected page afterwards does not display any event data.

issues.summary: A2 - Restrict functions to the roles permitted to use them
acceptanceCriteria: Every protected function has a defined list of the roles permitted to invoke it, and the same list governs what the interface offers and what the server accepts.

An attempt by a user whose role is not permitted is refused: the action does not execute, no record is created or modified, and the message states that the user's role is not authorised for that function.
The refusal applies to a direct URL or API call, not only to hidden menu items.
Navigation shows only the functions the signed-in user's role is permitted to use.
An unauthenticated request to any protected function is refused and returns no event, venue, equipment, or registration data.
issues.description:
Ref/ID: A2  
Component/Category: User Authentication & Authorisation  
**Goal:** Ensure features/actions are accessible only to permitted roles.  
**User Story:** As a ConnectSphere user, I want the system to stop me performing actions that belong to another role, so that I cannot damage an event by doing something I was never meant to do.  
**Acceptance Criteria:**

* Every protected function has a defined list of the roles permitted to invoke it, and the same list governs what the interface offers and what the server accepts.
* An attempt by a user whose role is not permitted is refused: the action does not execute, no record is created or modified, and the message states that the user's role is not authorised for that function.
* The refusal applies to a direct URL or API call, not only to hidden menu items.
* Navigation shows only the functions the signed-in user's role is permitted to use.
* An unauthenticated request to any protected function is refused and returns no event, venue, equipment, or registration data.

issues.summary: A3 - See only the events I am related to
acceptanceCriteria: An Event Organiser's event list contains only events where that organiser is the recorded owner.

An Event Coordinator's list contains **all events in the system**, and events **assigned to that coordinator are clearly distinguishable** from the rest (e.g., via an "Assigned to me" flag/filter/section).

Venue Staff see booking requests and confirmed bookings for their own venues, and the event details needed to assess them (name, timing, expected attendance, layout, requirements) — not the full internal event record.
Technical Support Staff see equipment requests and reservations, and the event timing they depend on.

An Attendee sees only events with registration enabled that are open to them, and only published fields — coordinator notes, review comments, clarification threads, and rejection reasons are excluded.
Filtering is applied when the list is retrieved, so a request for an event outside the user's relationship returns no event data at all.

issues.summary: B1 - Create and submit an event request
acceptanceCriteria: The request captures event name, purpose, description, proposed date, proposed start and end time, expected attendance, venue requirements, accessibility needs, equipment requirements, and whether attendee registration is required.
On a successful submission the request is stored with status Submitted, and the submitting organiser, submission timestamp, and a unique event reference are recorded and shown to the organiser.
The submitting organiser is recorded as the owner of the event.
The submitted request appears in the Event Coordinator review queue.
On submission the assigned coordinator (E1) is notified that a new event request is awaiting review.
If submission fails validation, no event record is created, no submission timestamp is recorded, and the entered values are preserved on screen.

issues.summary: B2 - Validate an event request before it is submitted
acceptanceCriteria: Submission is blocked unless event name, purpose, description, proposed date, start time, end time, expected attendance, and the registration-required flag are all populated.
When submission is blocked, the message names every field that caused the rejection, not just the first one.
The end date/time must be later than the start date/time; an equal or earlier end time is rejected and the message identifies this as the reason.
The proposed start date/time must not be in the past at the moment of submission.
Expected attendance must be a whole number greater than zero.
When registration is required:
**Registration opening date/time is mandatory**.
**Registration closing date/time is mandatory**.
Opening date/time must be earlier than closing date/time.
Closing date/time must be no later than the event start.
**Registration capacity is not entered directly; it is derived from the booked venue's capacity for the selected layout, and submission is blocked if this capacity cannot be retrieved.**
**An equipment-required flag is mandatory.** Selecting "none required" counts as a complete equipment arrangement for submission/confirmation purposes.
A blocked submission leaves the request at status Draft (or unsaved), creates no submission record, and changes no other stored value.
issues.description:
Ref/ID: B2  
Component/Category: Event Request Creation

**Goal:** Validate request data before submission.

**User Story:** As an Event Organiser, I want my event request validated before submission, so that incomplete or invalid data is caught and corrected early.

**Acceptance Criteria:**

* Submission is blocked unless event name, purpose, description, proposed date, start time, end time, expected attendance, and the registration-required flag are all populated.
* When submission is blocked, the message names every field that caused the rejection, not just the first one.
* The end date/time must be later than the start date/time; an equal or earlier end time is rejected and the message identifies this as the reason.
* The proposed start date/time must not be in the past at the moment of submission.
* Expected attendance must be a whole number greater than zero.
* When registration is required:

    * **Registration opening date/time is mandatory**.
    * **Registration closing date/time is mandatory**.
    * Opening date/time must be earlier than closing date/time.
    * Closing date/time must be no later than the event start.
    * **Registration capacity is not entered directly; it is derived from the booked venue's capacity for the selected layout, and submission is blocked if this capacity cannot be retrieved.**
    
* **An equipment-required flag is mandatory.** Selecting "none required" counts as a complete equipment arrangement for submission/confirmation purposes.
* A blocked submission leaves the request at status Draft (or unsaved), creates no submission record, and changes no other stored value.

**Dependencies / Blockers:**

* Blocked by Venue Service: booked-venue capacity lookup for selected layout.
* Blocked by Equipment Service: equipment readiness / arrangement-complete flag.

issues.summary: C1 - Save an incomplete event request as a draft
acceptanceCriteria: A request can be saved once the event name is present; every other field may be empty.

The submission validation rules in B2 are not applied on save, except that any date or time that is entered must be a valid date or time.
A draft does not appear in the Event Coordinator review queue and is not visible to any user other than its owner.
If the save fails, the previously saved version of the draft is unchanged and the last-saved timestamp is not updated.

issues.summary: D1 - Review the queue of submitted event requests

issues.summary: D2 - Request clarification from the organiser
acceptanceCriteria: A clarification message is mandatory and must contain at least one non-whitespace character; an empty message is refused, no message is stored, and the event status is unchanged.

The message is stored against the event and is visible to the owning organiser and to Event Coordinators; it is not visible to Attendees or Venue Staff.
The organiser receives a notification identifying the event and the fact that clarification is required.
Multiple clarification messages on the same event are retained in order rather than overwriting each other.

issues.summary: E1 - Assign an Event Coordinator to an event automatically
acceptanceCriteria: When an event is submitted, the system attempts to assign an Event Coordinator automatically.
Eligibility is determined from an **active/eligible coordinator pool** (e.g., active account + has Coordinator role); the assignment is made from that pool.
On successful assignment, the assigned coordinator, the assignment timestamp, and the assignment method (system-assigned) are recorded.
The assigned coordinator's name is shown to the owning organiser as the point of contact.
The assigned coordinator receives a notification identifying the event.

If there are **no eligible coordinators**, the event submission still succeeds, the event remains **unassigned**, and the event is placed into an **Awaiting assignment** state/queue visible to coordinators/admins.
An event has at most one active assigned coordinator at any time; creating a second active assignment is refused and names the current assignee.
issues.description:
Ref/ID: E1  
Component/Category: Coordinator Assignment

**Goal:** Automatically assign an event coordinator when an event is submitted.

**User Story:** As the system, I want to automatically assign an eligible Event Coordinator when an event is submitted, so that each submitted event has a clear coordinator owner without requiring manual assignment.

**Actor:** System (triggered by Event submission)

**Acceptance Criteria:**

* When an event is submitted, the system attempts to assign an Event Coordinator automatically.
* Eligibility is determined from an **active/eligible coordinator pool** (e.g., active account + has Coordinator role); the assignment is made from that pool.
* On successful assignment, the assigned coordinator, the assignment timestamp, and the assignment method (system-assigned) are recorded.
* The assigned coordinator's name is shown to the owning organiser as the point of contact.
* The assigned coordinator receives a notification identifying the event.
* If there are **no eligible coordinators**, the event submission still succeeds, the event remains **unassigned**, and the event is placed into an **Awaiting assignment** state/queue visible to coordinators/admins.
* An event has at most one active assigned coordinator at any time; creating a second active assignment is refused and names the current assignee.

**Dependencies / Blockers:**

* Blocked by Identity Service: eligible coordinator pool API (active + eligible coordinator list).

issues.summary: E2 - Reassign an event to a different coordinator
acceptanceCriteria: Reassignment proposals are permitted only for events not in status Completed, Cancelled, or Rejected.
A coordinator can **propose** reassignment by selecting a nominee coordinator.
The system verifies the nominee is eligible to be a coordinator (holds the Coordinator role); if not, the proposal is refused with a clear reason.
Only **one pending reassignment proposal** may exist per event at any time; creating a second proposal while one is pending is refused and identifies the pending nominee.
While a proposal is pending:
The **outgoing coordinator remains the active coordinator** and retains all coordinator actions.
The nominee does not gain coordinator actions until they accept.
The event shows a visible "Pending reassignment" state including nominee and proposed timestamp.
The nominee can **accept** or **decline** the proposal.
On **accept**:
The outgoing assignment is closed with an end timestamp and retained in assignment history.
A new active assignment is created for the nominee with a start timestamp.
Coordinator permissions/actions move to the nominee; the previous coordinator can no longer perform them.
Notifications are sent to outgoing and incoming coordinators; the owning organiser sees the updated point of contact.
On **decline**:
No assignment is changed; the outgoing coordinator remains active.
The proposal is closed/cleared and recorded in history (including declined outcome).
Notifications are sent to the relevant parties.
Proposing reassignment to the coordinator who is already assigned is refused and creates no new history entry.
issues.description:
Ref/ID: E2  
Component/Category: Coordinator Assignment

**Goal:** Allow reassignment of an event to a different coordinator via a propose → accept/decline handshake.

**User Story:** As an Event Coordinator, I want to propose reassignment of an event to another coordinator, so that responsibility can be transferred cleanly with explicit acceptance by the nominee.

**Acceptance Criteria:**

* Reassignment proposals are permitted only for events not in status Completed, Cancelled, or Rejected.
* A coordinator can **propose** reassignment by selecting a nominee coordinator.
* The system verifies the nominee is eligible to be a coordinator (holds the Coordinator role); if not, the proposal is refused with a clear reason.
* Only **one pending reassignment proposal** may exist per event at any time; creating a second proposal while one is pending is refused and identifies the pending nominee.
* While a proposal is pending:

    * The **outgoing coordinator remains the active coordinator** and retains all coordinator actions.
    * The nominee does not gain coordinator actions until they accept.
    * The event shows a visible "Pending reassignment" state including nominee and proposed timestamp.
    
* The nominee can **accept** or **decline** the proposal.
* On **accept**:

    * The outgoing assignment is closed with an end timestamp and retained in assignment history.
    * A new active assignment is created for the nominee with a start timestamp.
    * Coordinator permissions/actions move to the nominee; the previous coordinator can no longer perform them.
    * Notifications are sent to outgoing and incoming coordinators; the owning organiser sees the updated point of contact.
    
* On **decline**:

    * No assignment is changed; the outgoing coordinator remains active.
    * The proposal is closed/cleared and recorded in history (including declined outcome).
    * Notifications are sent to the relevant parties.
    
* Proposing reassignment to the coordinator who is already assigned is refused and creates no new history entry.

**Dependencies / Blockers:**

* Blocked by Identity Service: coordinator role check API (verify nominee holds Coordinator role).
* Related to E1 (SPM-24): shares assignment + history data model.

issues.summary: F1 - Trust that an event's status reflects what has actually happened
acceptanceCriteria: The permitted statuses are exactly: Draft, Submitted, Under Review, Awaiting Clarification, Approved, Planning, Safety Review, Confirmed, Completed, Cancelled, Rejected. ⚠ CR-06 adds Safety Review.
Status can only be changed by an action defined in another story; there is no screen that lets a user type or pick an arbitrary status.
An attempted transition that is not permitted from the current status is refused: no status change is stored, and the message names the current status and the attempted target.
Every status change writes a history entry containing previous status, new status, the acting user, their role, the timestamp, and the triggering action.

An event reaches Confirmed only through the confirmation action specified in F5, which defines the conditions that must hold. This story defines that Confirmed is a permitted status and that reaching it writes a history entry like any other transition. ⚠ **SPLIT — the readiness conditions moved to F5**

⚠ **CR-06:** F5's confirmation of the arrangements moves an event to Safety Review; only the Safety Officer's approval (U1) moves it to Confirmed, and a request for changes returns it to Planning. Each of these transitions writes a history entry like any other.
An event moves to Completed only after its recorded end date/time has passed.
issues.description:
Ref/ID: F1      
Component/Category: Event Status Management  
**Goal:** Move events through a controlled status lifecycle as a consequence of defined actions.  
**User Story:** As an Event Coordinator, I want an event's status to change only when something real has happened to it, so that I can rely on the status when deciding what to work on next.  
**Acceptance Criteria:**

* The permitted statuses are exactly: Draft, Submitted, Under Review, Awaiting Clarification, Approved, Planning, Safety Review, Confirmed, Completed, Cancelled, Rejected. ⚠ CR-06 adds Safety Review.
* Status can only be changed by an action defined in another story; there is no screen that lets a user type or pick an arbitrary status.
* An attempted transition that is not permitted from the current status is refused: no status change is stored, and the message names the current status and the attempted target.
* Every status change writes a history entry containing previous status, new status, the acting user, their role, the timestamp, and the triggering action.
* An event reaches Confirmed only through the confirmation action specified in F5, which defines the conditions that must hold. This story defines that Confirmed is a permitted status and that reaching it writes a history entry like any other transition. ⚠ **SPLIT — the readiness conditions moved to F5**
* ⚠ **CR-06:** F5's confirmation of the arrangements moves an event to Safety Review; only the Safety Officer's approval (U1) moves it to Confirmed, and a request for changes returns it to Planning. Each of these transitions writes a history entry like any other.
* An event moves to Completed only after its recorded end date/time has passed.

⚠ **REVISED by the Week 7 customer change CR-06** (`documentation/change-requests.md`, stories revision 4). Points are re-estimated at poker only if the team finds the change material.

acceptanceCriteria: A reservation records the event, equipment type, quantity reserved, reservation start and end date/time, the acting staff member, and the timestamp; the linked request line's status becomes Reserved.
The reservation is atomic with respect to the availability check: when two reservations for overlapping periods are processed simultaneously and only one unit remains, exactly one succeeds.

After a successful reservation the available quantity for any overlapping period is reduced by exactly the quantity reserved.
A quantity smaller than the requested quantity may be reserved only when explicitly chosen, and the reservation records the quantity actually reserved rather than the quantity requested.

issues.summary: R2 - Register for an event
acceptanceCriteria: A successful registration is stored with the attendee, the event, status Registered, and the registration timestamp, and the attendee sees a confirmation.

On success, places remaining decreases by exactly one; on any refusal it is unchanged.
The attendee receives a registration confirmation notification.

issues.description:
Tier 1 · Proposed sprint: 2 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 5    
Blocks: F5, F4, S2, S3, G2

**What it is:** The Identity and Event services merge into one program called `planning-core`, which will also hold Venue, Equipment and Change. Inside it, each part stays a separate module with its own folder, its own tables and a short list of functions other modules may call. "Boundary checks" (also called fitness functions) are automated tests in CI that fail the build if one module reaches into another's private files or tables.

**Why we need it:** F4 (cancel releases everything or nothing), F5 (confirm checks venue and equipment together), S3 (approve a change and flag bookings together) and G2 all need several modules to agree at once. With separate services, each of these becomes a saga with a window where things are half done.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Identity and Event run as one deployable `planning-core`, each a module with a public index.
* dependency-cruiser fails CI on cross-module internal imports.
* A check fails CI on SQL touching another module's schema.
* All A–E tests still pass, and `npm run dev` starts core and web.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "We run the staff side as one program so rules that span modules are one transaction, and CI stops modules from reaching into each other's code."

issues.summary: EN-03 — Event store and projections
acceptanceCriteria: An append-only `event_stream` with `unique(aggregate_id, version)` and a hash chain.
Projections update in the same transaction.
A–E data is migrated.
F1 and F2 history read from the stream.
A tamper check detects an edited entry.
issues.description:
Tier 2 · Proposed sprint: 2 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 8    
Blocks: F1, F2, G1, S2

**What it is:** Event sourcing: the system stops overwriting an event's details. It keeps an append-only list of everything that happened, such as "submitted by Alice at 10:02" or "attendance changed from 80 to 150 by Bob". The current state comes from replaying that list. Projections are ready-made tables built from the list, like the review queue, so screens stay fast. Each entry also stores a fingerprint (hash) of the previous one, so editing history later is detectable.

**Why we need it:** The briefing's auditability requirement (8f) asks who changed what, and when. F1's status history, F2's history screen, D3's "original values kept" and G1/S2's before-and-after values all come straight from the list and can never disagree with the current data.

**Acceptance criteria**

* An append-only `event_stream` with `unique(aggregate_id, version)` and a hash chain.
* Projections update in the same transaction.
* A–E data is migrated.
* F1 and F2 history read from the stream.
* A tamper check detects an edited entry.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "An event's history is the data itself, so the audit trail can't drift away from what actually happened."

Decision record: ADR-0007. Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

---

issues.summary: EN-04 — Kafka messaging done safely
acceptanceCriteria: Hosted Kafka chosen (an ADR records why).
Topics per aggregate, keyed by aggregate id.

The relay uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.
The notification consumer has an inbox table, retry topics and a DLQ.

issues.description:
Tier 1 · Proposed sprint: 2 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 5    
Blocks: T2 and every notification acceptance criterion

Provider setup is already tracked in SPM-113 (5 pts, Sprint 2). Size only the remaining scope when you poker this.

**What it is:** The pieces that make messages reliable: Kafka, the shared message log; CloudEvents, a standard envelope so every message carries the same id, type, source and time; an inbox table where each reader records the messages it has already handled; retry topics, where a failed message waits and is tried again later; and a dead-letter queue, where messages go after repeated failure so a person can inspect and replay them.

**Why we need it:** T2 and every notification acceptance criterion (B1, D2 to D5, E1, E2, F3, M1 and more). In Sprint 1 the messages were saved but never sent.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Hosted Kafka chosen (an ADR records why).
* Topics per aggregate, keyed by aggregate id.
* CloudEvents envelope validated by `contracts`.
* The relay uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.
* The notification consumer has an inbox table, retry topics and a DLQ.
* Tests: a duplicate message creates one notification, and broker downtime loses nothing.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "Messages can arrive twice, and our inbox makes processing them twice harmless."

Decision record: ADR-0008. Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: EN-05 — CDC and schema registry
acceptanceCriteria: Spike first: confirm Supabase allows a logical replication slot.
Debezium outbox router replaces the relay.
CI checks backward compatibility against the schema registry.
issues.description:
Tier 2 · Proposed sprint: 2 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 3    
Relates to: EN-04 (improves it)

**What it is:** Postgres writes every committed change to its own log, the write-ahead log (WAL). Change data capture (CDC) reads that log and turns new outbox rows into Kafka messages; Debezium is the standard tool for it. A schema registry is a catalogue of the exact shape of every message type, and CI checks each change against it.

**Why we need it:** Less code we have to write and debug ourselves: it replaces a hand-written relay that polls the database. It also supports the briefing's maintainability requirement (8g): new message versions can't silently break old readers.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Spike first: confirm Supabase allows a logical replication slot.
* Debezium outbox router replaces the relay.
* CI checks backward compatibility against the schema registry.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "We don't poll for messages. We read the database's own commit log, and a registry blocks breaking changes to message formats."

Decision record: ADR-0008. Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

---

## Start here

**Tier 2, so take it last. Blocked by EN-04.2** (SPM-166). The relay must work before anything replaces it.

1. **Spike first, about an hour.** Check whether the team's Supabase plan allows a logical replication slot for an external Debezium connector, and whether your Kafka provider offers managed Kafka Connect.
2. **If either answer is no,** close this item as "won't do" with a comment. Add one line to ADR-0008 saying the polling relay stays and why. That's a legitimate, recorded trade-off, not a failure.
3. **If both are yes,** set up the Debezium outbox event router, and add a schema registry check to CI.

**Done when:** either the spike result is recorded and the item is closed, or the acceptance criteria above hold. Either way, there's a CHANGELOG entry. Process: `documentation/planning/definition-of-ready.md`.

issues.summary: EN-06 — CI pipeline v1
acceptanceCriteria: GitHub Actions on every PR runs lint, typecheck, unit tests with 100% domain coverage, Stryker on the domain (≥ 80%), integration tests on an ephemeral Postgres (never the shared DB), squawk, CodeQL and gitleaks.

issues.description:
Tier 1 · Proposed sprint: 2 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 5    
Blocks: all stories (Definition of Done), and EN-21

GitHub Actions, branch protection and coverage are already tracked in SPM-114, SPM-115 and SPM-116 (7 pts, Sprint 2). Size only the remaining scope when you poker this.

**What it is:** GitHub Actions runs a fixed set of checks on every pull request: lint and typecheck; unit tests with coverage, plus mutation testing; integration tests against a throwaway Postgres, so tests never touch the team's shared database; a migration linter (squawk) that flags risky schema changes; and code security scanning (CodeQL) plus gitleaks, which catches passwords committed by accident. Mutation testing plants small bugs, such as changing `>` to `>=`, then checks that some test fails.

**Why we need it:** The rubric's "Code quality and CI" row asks for a comprehensive pipeline that reliably builds and tests the system, and the repo currently has none. Mutation testing backs up "100% coverage" by proving the tests actually assert things.

**Acceptance criteria**

* GitHub Actions on every PR runs lint, typecheck, unit tests with 100% domain coverage, Stryker on the domain (≥ 80%), integration tests on an ephemeral Postgres (never the shared DB), squawk, CodeQL and gitleaks.
* Branch protection requires it.
* The ubuntu runner's preinstalled Postgres avoids Docker.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "Every pull request runs the same gates automatically, and mutation testing proves our tests actually catch bugs."

Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: EN-07 — Permission policies and row-level security
acceptanceCriteria: Cerbos policies in the repo, evaluated by the gateway, services and SPA navigation.

issues.description:
Tier 1 · Proposed sprint: 2 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 5

**What it is:** Cerbos is a policy engine: permission rules like "an Event Coordinator may approve an event" are files in the repo, and the gateway, the backend and the UI all ask the same engine. Row-level security (RLS) is a Postgres feature that filters which rows a user may see on every query, automatically. The authorization matrix is a generated test that tries every role on every endpoint, with both related and unrelated records.

**Why we need it:** The briefing's security requirement (8b). A3 is exactly OWASP's number one API risk, broken object level authorization: seeing records you're not related to.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Cerbos policies in the repo, evaluated by the gateway, services and SPA navigation.
* A3 enforced with RLS, using a per-request role and `SET LOCAL` claims inside each transaction.
* A generated matrix test covers role × endpoint × related and unrelated resources.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "Permissions live in one policy file used everywhere, and the database itself hides events you're not related to."

Blocks: F1, F4, R6, S3, EN-20

Note: F1 is in Sprint 2 but its "Completed after the end time" criterion needs this Sprint 3 timer. Raise it at the Sprint 2 review.

**What it is:** A workflow engine. It runs multi-step processes and records every completed step. If the server crashes halfway, the process continues from the last recorded step on another server. It also offers reliable timers ("at the event's end time, do X") and automatic retries.

**Why we need it:** F4 needs all-or-nothing across the core and the registration service. F1 needs a scheduler, and the current plan's "Scheduled Job Runner" has no owner and no story.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Temporal workers.
* A CompleteEvent timer (F1).
* A CancelEvent workflow with a semantic lock (freeze, commit, finalise, with unfreeze on failure).
* Time-skipping tests and replay tests in CI.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "Long processes like cancellation survive crashes, because every step is recorded and resumed where it stopped."

Decision record: ADR-0009. Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: EN-12 — API gateway, rate limits, CDN
acceptanceCriteria: Kong with the JWT plugin against the Supabase JWKS.
Per-user and per-IP rate limits backed by Redis.
Trace headers.
Separate staff and public routes.
CDN in front of the SPA and the browse API.
issues.description:
Tier 2 · Proposed sprint: 3 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 5  
Blocks: R1, R2, EN-19

**What it is:** The API gateway (Kong) is the single front door. It checks login tokens, routes each request to the right program, and applies rate limits: a cap on how many requests each user or IP address can make per second. The counters live in Redis, so every gateway copy sees the same count. A CDN is a network of servers near users that keeps copies of the website and the public event list.

**Why we need it:** The briefing's performance (8a) and scalability (8e) requirements. The plan already lists a gateway, but it was never built; the web app currently uses a development proxy.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Kong with the JWT plugin against the Supabase JWKS.
* Per-user and per-IP rate limits backed by Redis.
* Trace headers.
* Separate staff and public routes.
* CDN in front of the SPA and the browse API.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "The gateway is the front door. It checks who you are and how fast you're allowed to knock."

Decision record: ADR-0011. Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: EN-13 — Registration service and seat inventory
acceptanceCriteria: Its own service and database.
A `seats` table claimed with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, with public and VIP pools.
Seats created from `booking.confirmed`.
Attendee PWA shell.
issues.description:
Tier 1 · Proposed sprint: 3 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 5  
Blocks: R1 to R7, EN-18, EN-20

**What it is:** Registration becomes its own program with its own database. Each event gets one database row per seat, and registering means claiming any free row with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` ("give me a row nobody else is holding, and don't wait for the busy ones"). Seats are split into a public pool and a VIP pool. The attendee site is a PWA (progressive web app) that installs like an app on a phone and shows "my registrations" offline.

**Why we need it:** R2 requires the capacity check and the registration to be atomic. The VIP pool fixes the R2 and R7 contradiction (see CQ-01). The briefing requires mobile access for attendees.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Its own service and database.
* A `seats` table claimed with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, with public and VIP pools.
* Seats created from `booking.confirmed`.
* Attendee PWA shell.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "Each seat is a row, so the database can never hand out seat 101, and nobody waits in line behind one counter."

Decision record: ADR-0005. Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: EN-14 — Preview environments and browser tests
acceptanceCriteria: A per-PR preview (or ephemeral CI stack).
Playwright E2E tagged with story test ids.
axe accessibility checks.
Visual snapshots at 360, 768 and 1280 px.

On that copy, Playwright clicks through real user journeys end to end, axe checks accessibility (contrast, labels, keyboard use, WCAG AA), and screenshots at phone, tablet and desktop widths are compared to approved ones (visual regression testing).

**Why we need it:** The rubric's testing row asks for end-to-end tests. The briefing asks for usability and mobile access. It also ends "works on my machine".

* A per-PR preview (or ephemeral CI stack).
* Playwright E2E tagged with story test ids.
* axe accessibility checks.
* Visual snapshots at 360, 768 and 1280 px.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "Every pull request gets its own live copy that robots click through at phone, tablet and desktop sizes."

acceptanceCriteria: OpenFeature with flagd.
Flag `change-approval` gates S2 approval in production.

Blocks: S1, S2

**What it is:** An on/off switch for a feature, kept in configuration, so it can be enabled without redeploying. OpenFeature is the standard way to read these switches.

**Why we need it:** S1 and S2 (change requests) can merge in Sprint 3 while staying switched off in production, and switch on in Sprint 4 once S3 can flag the bookings a change affects. Approving a change that ignores existing bookings would break the customer's rules.

issues.summary: EN-16 — Canary releases
acceptanceCriteria: Argo Rollouts canary at 10, 50 and 100%, with Prometheus analysis of error rate and p95.
Automatic rollback demonstrated.
issues.description:
Tier 2 · Proposed sprint: 4 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 3  
Needs: EN-10

**What it is:** A new version first receives 10% of real traffic, then 50%, then 100%. At each stage the system compares error rate and response time with the SLO, and rolls back automatically if the new version is worse.

**Why we need it:** Zero-downtime, low-risk delivery is part of what the ESM finalists were recognised for. A bad release affects a few users for a minute instead of everyone for an hour.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Argo Rollouts canary at 10, 50 and 100%, with Prometheus analysis of error rate and p95.
* Automatic rollback demonstrated.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "New versions are tried on a small slice of users first, and pulled back automatically if they misbehave."

Decision record: ADR-0012. Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: EN-17 — SLOs, alerts, dashboards, runbooks
acceptanceCriteria: SLOs written down: registration p95 ≤ 800 ms at 500 req/s, zero over-admission, staff p95, notification freshness within 10 s, 99.9% availability.
Burn-rate alerts and a runbook per alert.
issues.description:
Tier 1 · Proposed sprint: 4 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 3  
Needs: EN-08

**What it is:** An SLO is a measurable promise, such as "95% of registrations complete within 0.8 seconds". The error budget is how much failure that promise allows (99.9% a month is about 43 minutes). A burn-rate alert fires when the budget is being used up too quickly. A runbook is step-by-step fix instructions for each alert.

**Why we need it:** It turns the briefing's "complete within a reasonable time" into numbers the team measures and reports. The rubric rewards demonstrable, reliable software.

**Acceptance criteria**

* SLOs written down: registration p95 ≤ 800 ms at 500 req/s, zero over-admission, staff p95, notification freshness within 10 s, 99.9% availability.
* Burn-rate alerts and a runbook per alert.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "We set numeric targets for speed and uptime, and alert ourselves before we break them."

Decision record: ADR-0013. Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: EN-18 — Load tests and autoscaling
acceptanceCriteria: k6 spike test (500 req/s for 100 seats gives exactly 100 registered), soak and stress tests.
Autoscaling tuned.
Results committed as evidence.
issues.description:
Tier 1 · Proposed sprint: 4 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 3  
Needs: EN-13

**What it is:** k6 is a load-testing tool that simulates many users. A spike test sends a sudden burst, like registration opening; a soak test keeps a steady load for hours to find slow leaks. Autoscaling adds copies of a program when CPU or backlog rises (HPA for the APIs, KEDA for Kafka readers), and tuning sets its limits from the test results.

**Why we need it:** The briefing's scalability requirement (8e) asks for three years of growth. This proves it with numbers instead of claims.

**Acceptance criteria**

* k6 spike test (500 req/s for 100 seats gives exactly 100 registered), soak and stress tests.
* Autoscaling tuned.
* Results committed as evidence.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "We don't claim it scales. We hit it with 500 requests a second and publish the results."

Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: EN-19 — Virtual waiting room
acceptanceCriteria: Admission tokens for events flagged high-demand, at the tested rate.
issues.description:
Tier 2 · Proposed sprint: 4 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 2  
Needs: EN-12

**What it is:** For events marked high-demand, arriving attendees take a place in a queue. They're let in at the rate the system has been tested to handle, the way concert ticket sites work.

**Why we need it:** Registration opening is the only real traffic spike in this business. It keeps that spike inside tested capacity and orders people fairly by arrival. It's a showcase item, so it's the first to cut.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Admission tokens for events flagged high-demand, at the tested rate.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "For popular events, people queue fairly instead of all hitting the server at the same second."

Decision record: ADR-0011. Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: EN-20 — Chaos experiments
acceptanceCriteria: Six experiments (architecture page §7), each with a hypothesis, result and fix log.
Toxiproxy in CI.
issues.description:
Tier 1 · Proposed sprint: 4 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 3  
Needs: EN-04, EN-11, EN-13

**What it is:** Chaos engineering: deliberately breaking parts of the system in a controlled way, such as stopping a server, cutting off Kafka or slowing the database. Each experiment starts with a written hypothesis of what should happen and ends with a record of what actually did. For example, kill the core in the middle of a cancellation and check that the result is still all or nothing.

**Why we need it:** The rubric's top band asks for "failure scenarios". This is exactly how the ESM finalist proved their system heals itself.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Six experiments (architecture page §7), each with a hypothesis, result and fix log.
* Toxiproxy in CI.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "We break things on purpose, write down what should happen, and show that it does."

Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §7 and §13b.

issues.summary: EN-21 — Software supply chain security
acceptanceCriteria: SBOM, cosign signatures, Trivy and a ZAP baseline scan in the pipeline.
issues.description:
Tier 2 · Proposed sprint: 4 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 3  
Needs: EN-06, EN-10

**What it is:** An SBOM (software bill of materials) lists every library inside the build. cosign digitally signs container images, so the cluster runs only images the team built. Trivy scans images for known vulnerabilities. ZAP acts as an automated attacker, probing the running preview site for common web flaws.

**Why we need it:** The briefing's security requirement (8b). You know exactly what ships, tampered or vulnerable images are blocked, and common web attacks are tried against every change.

**Acceptance criteria**

* SBOM, cosign signatures, Trivy and a ZAP baseline scan in the pipeline.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "We know every library we ship, we sign what we build, and we scan it before it runs."

Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: EN-22 — Traceability generator and DORA dashboard
acceptanceCriteria: Generates the story → AC → test → last-result matrix from test tags on every CI run.
Tracks the four DORA metrics.
issues.description:
Tier 1 · Proposed sprint: 4 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 3  
Blocks: Deliverable 3 (traceability)

**What it is:** Each automated test is tagged with its story and test-case id, for example `@R2-T3`. On every CI run, a script reads the tags and the stories file, then writes the story, criterion, test and latest-result table. DORA metrics are four research-backed measures of delivery: how often you deploy, how long a change takes to reach users, how often a change breaks something, and how fast you recover.

**Why we need it:** The rubric's testing and traceability row, and its scrum row's "refined using evidence". It also fixes the Sprint 1 problem of points and lists drifting between documents.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Generates the story → AC → test → last-result matrix from test tags on every CI run.
* Tracks the four DORA metrics.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "Our traceability matrix builds itself from test tags on every run, and our retros use real delivery metrics."

Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: EN-23 — Threat model, PDPA review, ASVS checklist
acceptanceCriteria: A STRIDE table per container, a PDPA note on attendee data, and an ASVS Level 2 checklist mapped to controls.
issues.description:
Tier 1 · Proposed sprint: 4 · Proposed estimate (to be poker'd): 2  
Blocks: Deliverable 2 (system design)

**What it is:** STRIDE is a method for listing threats to each part of the system: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. PDPA is Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act, which covers attendee names and emails. ASVS is OWASP's checklist of security requirements; Level 2 is recommended for apps holding personal data.

**Why we need it:** It shows security was designed in rather than bolted on (briefing 8b), and it gives clear answers if Week 13 asks "what stops X?".

**Acceptance criteria**

* A STRIDE table per container, a PDPA note on attendee data, and an ASVS Level 2 checklist mapped to controls.

**In the Week 13 Q&A:** "We listed how the system could be attacked and how each attack is blocked, and we handle attendee data under PDPA."

Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §5; target architecture page §13b.

issues.summary: PX-01 — Make Jira the single source of story points
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** PO

**Done when:** Sprint 1 is restated as 35 in `plan.md`, `documentation/sprint allocation.csv` and `CHANGELOG.md`, with a note on the earlier figures.

**Why:** Sprint 1 appears as 34 (the planning transcript's total), 35 (the poker votes, and what Jira holds), 44 (plan.md "planned"), 47 (plan.md and the CSV "delivered") and 52 (CHANGELOG). The document estimates (A3 = 5, B2 = 5) don't match the poker votes (A3 = 1, B2 = 2).

**Status note (1 Oct 2026):** the repo documents were restated to Jira's numbers on 1 Oct, with a correction note (see CHANGELOG). The PO checks the result, then closes this.

Source: documentation/proposals/2026-10-01-target-architecture-and-jira-plan.md §6; sprint evidence playbook §6, gap 1.

issues.summary: PX-02 — Re-estimate Sprint 2–4 stories and enablers with planning poker
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** Whole team

**Done when:** A recorded planning-poker session. For every item, the lowest and highest vote plus the reason are noted, and the agreed points are written to Jira's Story point estimate field.

**Scope:**

* Sprint 3 and 4 stories, which have no points in Jira yet (only F5 = 5 and F3 = 3 do).
* P1, which moved into Sprint 2 without points.
* EN-01 to EN-23. Each carries a "Proposed estimate (to be poker'd)" in its description; those are starting points for discussion, not estimates. EN-04 and EN-06 overlap SPM-113 to 116, so size only their remaining scope.

**Why:** The Week 3 slides say "don't outsource the estimate". The playbook also says to point platform enablers, because the slides allow infrastructure work "if the work contributes towards the Product Goal".

**Template (estimates table for the planning record):**

```
## Estimates (planning poker, reference story <ID> = <pts>)
| Story | Votes low–high | Agreed | Why | Owner |
```

Source: plan §6; playbook §6, gaps 1 and 4.

issues.summary: PX-03 — Estimation reference
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** PO + SM

**Done when:** A reference story (suggest C1 = 2) and a one-line meaning for 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8, kept in Confluence or the repo and cited at the top of every planning record.

**Why:** The Sprint 1 planning transcript shows poker votes, but there's no reference story, no definition of what each point value means, and no written reason per story. Both past example teams had a baseline story and a points matrix.

Source: plan §6; playbook §2 and §6, gap 4.

issues.summary: PX-04 — Standup log
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** SM

**Done when:** A sheet or Confluence table with a date, sprint and day number on every row. Two live 15-minute calls a week, plus written entries on the other working days (done, next, blockers, goal on track). Not back-filled for Sprint 1; instead, say in the Sprint 2 review and retro that logging started, which is itself visible adaptation.

**Why:** The repo holds no standup entries, and day-to-day status goes to Telegram. If you stay on Telegram, use the fixed format below in a dedicated topic and have the SM copy it into the log weekly.

**Template (one entry per person):**

```
<date> · Sprint N · day <d> · <name> (<role>)
Done since last update:
Next, until the next update:
Blockers or help needed:
Sprint goal: on track / at risk because <reason>
```

Source: plan §6; playbook §3 (daily scrum) and §6, gap 2.

issues.summary: PX-05 — Sprint 2 planning record
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** SM + PO

**Done when:** The Sprint 2 planning record is written from what was agreed (roles, goal, dates, capacity, stories, points, owners, risks, carry-over) and honestly dated as written up later, e.g. "recorded on <date> from the 22 Sep decisions". It includes the mid-sprint change of 1 Oct (enablers and PX tasks added, F3 out, P1 in).

**Template:**

```
# Sprint N planning · <date>
Roles: PO <name> · SM <name> · Developers <names>
Dates: <start> to <end> (<n> working days)
Sprint goal: <one sentence: the outcome, not a list of stories>

## Capacity and velocity
|                               | This sprint | Last sprint |
| Available person-days         |             |             |
| Planned points                |             |             |
| Completed points (Done only)  | n/a         |             |
Why this amount: <tie it to last velocity, absences, midterms>

## Estimates (planning poker, reference story <ID> = <pts>)
| Story | Votes low–high | Agreed | Why | Owner |

## Carried over
| Story | Why not Done | Re-estimated? |

## Changed requirements since last sprint
<what changed, which clarification (C-nn), which stories>

## Risks
| Risk | Mitigation | Owner |
```

Source: plan §6; playbook §6, gap 5, and §8.

issues.summary: PX-06 — Burndown and velocity
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** SM

**Done when:**

* Jira Reports are enabled.
* On the last day of each sprint, a sprint burndown screenshot plus a two-sentence reading (velocity, points left against the ideal line, and why).
* An across-sprint burndown sheet starting from Sprint 1 = 35, raising the line whenever scope grows (T1 removed; F4, L3, R6, R7 added; enablers added on 1 Oct).
* From Sprint 2 onward, Jira's velocity report.

**Note:** Sprint 2 was only started in Jira on 1 Oct 2026 (start date kept as 23 Sep), so its burndown begins then. The enablers and PX tasks added on 1 Oct will show as scope added mid-sprint, which is accurate.

**Example reading:** "Velocity 35. Most points landed in the last three days because stories were only marked Done after review, so next sprint we mark Done as each story passes its tests."

Source: plan §6; playbook §4 and §6, gap 3.

issues.summary: PX-07 — Customer clarification log
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** PO

**Done when:** `documentation/clarifications.md` exists with C-01 onwards (question, answer, decision, stories changed), including the C-04 and C-10 to C-13 already cited in the stories, and the answers to CQ-01 to CQ-03 once they arrive.

**Why:** The stories rubric's top band asks for "conversations, constraints … and changed requirements", and this log is that evidence. The stories cite clarifications whose questions and answers aren't recorded anywhere.

**Template:**

```
C-<nn> · <date> · asked by <name> · <Q&A session>
Question:
Customer's answer (as close to verbatim as possible):
Decision:
Stories and acceptance criteria changed: <IDs>
Backlog updated by <name> on <date>
```

Source: plan §6; playbook §6, gap 8, and §8.

issues.summary: PX-08 — Review record with demo log and proxy feedback
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** PO

**Done when:** The template below is used from the Sprint 2 review onward. The PO attends as the customer's proxy and their feedback is recorded. Each demo is logged with the account, steps, result, test-case ID and a screenshot. The test-case execution records can double as demo scripts.

**Why:** The Sprint 1 review is well written, but it records "stakeholder feedback: not applicable" and has no demo log or screenshots. The slides warn against the review becoming "a demo/status presentation rather than collaborative inspection".

**Template:**

```
# Sprint N review · <date>
Attendees: <team> · stakeholder or proxy: <name>
Sprint goal met? yes / partly / no. Evidence: <…>

## Done (meets DoD vN)       <Jira screenshot>
## Not done
| Story | Why | Back to backlog as |

## Demo log
| Story | Account | Steps | Result | Test case | Screenshot |

## Feedback
| From | Feedback | Backlog change |

## Numbers
Planned <x> · completed <y> (Done only)
Burndown: <chart>. Reading: <two sentences>
```

Source: plan §6; playbook §3 (sprint review), §6, gap 6, and §8.

issues.summary: PX-09 — Retro follow-up
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** SM

**Done when:** Every retro opens by reviewing the last one's actions: done or not, did it help, and the evidence. For example, did the fixed Wednesday slot actually raise attendance? Switching retro format once (start-stop-continue to 4Ls) is itself evidence of adapting.

**Why:** The Sprint 1 retro already has start, stop and continue with an owned action table, which is better than both example teams. The follow-up table is the proof of "visible improvement across sprints".

**Template:**

```
# Sprint N retrospective · <date>
Format: start-stop-continue / 4Ls / <other>

## Last sprint's actions
| Action | Owner | Done? | Did it help? Evidence |

## Board          <screenshot, names on rows>

## Next sprint's improvements (2 to 3)
| Action | Owner | How we'll know it worked |
```

Source: plan §6; playbook §3 (retrospective), §6, gap 7, and §8.

issues.summary: PX-10 — AI-usage log
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** All

**Done when:** A short entry per story or task: what the AI produced, what a human reviewed or changed, and who. It's kept in each sprint folder (`09-ai-usage.md`).

**Why:** The rubric's top band says "articulately justifies trade-offs and AI contributions". The team builds with coding agents, so a short log per story turns that into evidence. The Week 3 slides add that AI "doesn't replace the feedback loops" of the scrum events.

**Template:**

```
Sprint N · <story or task> · tool: <e.g. Claude Code>
AI produced:
Human reviewed or changed:
Reviewed by: <name> · PR / commit: <link>
```

Source: plan §6; playbook §3 (continuous), §6, gap 10, and §8.

issues.summary: PX-11 — Roles per sprint
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** Team

**Done when:** Every planning record starts with a roles table (PO, SM, developers). The Sprint 2 PO is named, following the rotation agreed at the Sprint 1 retro.

**Why:** No one has been named PO for Sprint 2 yet. The customer questions CQ-01 to CQ-03 go to the PO, and the Gate B sign-off on the 1 Oct story moves should record who acted as PO.

Source: plan §6; playbook §6, gap 10.

issues.summary: PX-12 — Sprint 4 recordings plan
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** SM

**Done when:** Four separate sessions are booked (planning, one standup, review, retro), recorded, and uploaded as unlisted videos with the links in the submission. Don't combine review and retro.

**What should be visible on camera:**

* **Sprint planning:** the PO presenting ordered items; live planning poker with hidden votes, then the high and low voters explaining; capacity against last velocity; the goal agreed; stories split into subtasks.
* **One daily standup:** under 15 minutes; each developer talks about the sprint goal with the Jira board on screen; a blocker gets taken offline with a named person.
* **Sprint review:** the demo driven by test cases, feedback being taken, a backlog item changed live, velocity and burndown shown.
* **Retrospective:** last sprint's actions checked first, then the board, then two or three owned actions.

Sprint 4 runs 21 Oct to 3 Nov 2026.

Source: plan §6; playbook §5.

issues.summary: PX-13 — Week 7 consultation questions

2. Can the Product Owner act as the customer's proxy in sprint reviews, given no external stakeholder attends?

4. Should infrastructure work (CI, Kafka relay, test kit) be pointed backlog items that count toward velocity?
5. Is an across-sprint burndown built in a sheet from Jira data the format you want?
6. How detailed should the per-story demo evidence in the review be?

issues.summary: PX-14 — Changed-requirements note
issues.description:
**Suggested owner:** PO

**Done when:** The next planning record has a "Handling evolving requirements" section: what changed, why, and how it was re-estimated and re-planned. At minimum: T1 removed; F1 and F3 split (F5 and F4 added); L3, R6 and R7 added; the 1 Oct story moves (F3 → Sprint 4, P1 → Sprint 2, F5 → Sprint 3, R1 → Sprint 4); and any answers to CQ-01 to CQ-03.

issues.summary: CQ-01 — R7 VIP adds versus registration places
issues.description:

issues.summary: H3 - Set a venue's setup and turnaround time
acceptanceCriteria: A venue records a setup time and a turnaround time, each a whole number of minutes, zero or greater; any other value is refused and stores nothing.

An event's occupied period at a venue runs from its start minus the setup time to its end plus the turnaround time. For example, an event from 10:00 to 12:00 with 30 minutes' setup and 45 minutes' turnaround occupies the venue from 09:30 to 12:45.

Availability, holds, booking approval, conflict flags and unavailability blocks compare occupied periods, not the advertised start and end times (I1, I2, J1, L3, M1, N1, N2). Occupied periods that merely touch do not overlap.

When a venue's setup or turnaround time changes, every hold, pending request and confirmed booking at that venue whose occupied period would now overlap another is identified. Each is flagged Requires Reconfirmation with the reason and the overlapping reference, and its coordinator is notified. None is removed, released, or moved.
Each change records the acting user, the timestamp, and the previous and new values.
Only Venue Staff can change setup and turnaround times (A2).

Ref/ID: H3    
Component/Category: Venue Catalogue    
⚠ **NEW — Week 7 change CR-01** (`documentation/change-requests.md`)

**Goal:** Each venue has a configurable setup and turnaround time, included whenever availability or conflicts are checked.

**User Story:** As a Venue Staff member, I want to record how long my venue needs to be prepared before an event and reset after it, so that bookings always leave that time free.

**Acceptance Criteria:**

* A venue records a setup time and a turnaround time, each a whole number of minutes, zero or greater; any other value is refused and stores nothing.
* An event's occupied period at a venue runs from its start minus the setup time to its end plus the turnaround time. For example, an event from 10:00 to 12:00 with 30 minutes' setup and 45 minutes' turnaround occupies the venue from 09:30 to 12:45.
* Availability, holds, booking approval, conflict flags and unavailability blocks compare occupied periods, not the advertised start and end times (I1, I2, J1, L3, M1, N1, N2). Occupied periods that merely touch do not overlap.
* When a venue's setup or turnaround time changes, every hold, pending request and confirmed booking at that venue whose occupied period would now overlap another is identified. Each is flagged Requires Reconfirmation with the reason and the overlapping reference, and its coordinator is notified. None is removed, released, or moved.
* Each change records the acting user, the timestamp, and the previous and new values.
* Only Venue Staff can change setup and turnaround times (A2).

---

**Design:**

* ADR-0006 already uses `blocked_period = [start − setup, end + turnaround)` in the exclusion constraint, so this is data, not structure.
* When the buffers change, don't rewrite stored periods; flag the conflicts instead (`implementation.md` §4.6).
* The venue gains `setup_minutes` and `turnaround_minutes`, so build H1's tables with them.
* Whether buffers apply to holds and blocks is CQ-09.

issues.summary: I3 - Return a Confirmed event to Planning when its venue is blocked
acceptanceCriteria: When a block (I2) disrupts a confirmed booking of an event in status Confirmed, the event's status becomes Planning, with a status history entry naming the block as the triggering action (F1). An event in any other status is unchanged, as in I2.
The event and its record are kept: it is never cancelled, and its other arrangements and registrations are unchanged.
The assigned coordinator is notified at once, as in I2, and the notification states that the event has returned to Planning.

The owning organiser and the registered attendees are not notified when the block is recorded. They are notified when a replacement booking is approved (L5, M1) or a change to the event is approved (S2).
To become Confirmed again, the event passes confirmation (F5) and the safety check (U1) again, as after any other return to Planning.
A failed block creation changes no event's status (I2).
issues.description:
Ref/ID: I3  
Component/Category: Venue Availability Calendar  
⚠ **NEW — Week 9 answers (W9-FX-1)**, `documentation/clarifications.md`

**Change:** a new requirement on a Done story (course guide, scenario 2). I2 (SPM-35) stays Done; this story replaces I2's "the corresponding event's status is unchanged" for a Confirmed event.

**User Story:** As an assigned Event Coordinator, I want a Confirmed event whose venue becomes unavailable to go back to Planning, so that it is re-planned and checked again before it goes ahead.

**Acceptance Criteria**

* When a block (I2) disrupts a confirmed booking of an event in status Confirmed, the event's status becomes Planning, with a status history entry naming the block as the triggering action (F1). An event in any other status is unchanged, as in I2.
* The event and its record are kept: it is never cancelled, and its other arrangements and registrations are unchanged.
* The assigned coordinator is notified at once, as in I2, and the notification states that the event has returned to Planning.
* The owning organiser and the registered attendees are not notified when the block is recorded. They are notified when a replacement booking is approved (L5, M1) or a change to the event is approved (S2).
* To become Confirmed again, the event passes confirmation (F5) and the safety check (U1) again, as after any other return to Planning.
* A failed block creation changes no event's status (I2).

**Source:** "Should revert to Planning review. The event itself is preserve and not automatically cancelled" (W9-50); "The Event Coordinator is informed immediately … Organisers and Attendees are notified when replacement arrangements or formal event changes are confirmed" (W9-51); W9-43.

**Design and tests to update:** event status machine (new transition Confirmed → Planning), sequence diagram for a block, notification wording; regression tests on I2 and F1.

1. Backend: transactionally reset disrupted Confirmed events to Planning; record block; notify coordinator.
2. Frontend: show block in history.
3. Tests: Confirmed transition, other-status unchanged, failure rollback.

issues.summary: I4 - Refuse a hold over a blocked period
acceptanceCriteria: Requesting or placing a tentative hold (L3) whose occupied period (H3) overlaps an active block is refused. The refusal names the block, its period and its reason type, and nothing is stored. Periods that merely touch do not overlap.
Holds already requested or placed when a block is created are flagged, not refused or released, as in I2.
Once the block is removed, holds over its period can be requested and placed again.
issues.description:
Ref/ID: I4  
Component/Category: Venue Availability Calendar  
⚠ **NEW — Week 9 answers (W9-FX-2)**, `documentation/clarifications.md`

**Change:** a new requirement on Done stories (course guide, scenario 2). I2 (SPM-35) and L3 (SPM-110) stay Done; I2 already refuses new booking requests over a block, and this adds holds.

**User Story:** As a Venue Staff member, I want a block to stop new holds as well as new booking requests, so that nobody reserves a period the venue cannot offer.

**Acceptance Criteria**

* Requesting or placing a tentative hold (L3) whose occupied period (H3) overlaps an active block is refused. The refusal names the block, its period and its reason type, and nothing is stored. Periods that merely touch do not overlap.
* Holds already requested or placed when a block is created are flagged, not refused or released, as in I2.
* Once the block is removed, holds over its period can be requested and placed again.

**Source:** "Marking a venue unavailable for hold blocks new holds and bookings, and flags affected existing bookings so alternative venues can be arranged" (W9-41).

issues.summary: I5 - Record a block with no end
acceptanceCriteria: A block may be created with no end date and time; it stays active until Venue Staff remove it (I2). When an end is given, it must still be later than the start, as in I2.
An open-ended block disrupts and flags, as in I2, every confirmed booking, pending request and hold at the venue whose occupied period ends after the block starts.
From its start, an open-ended block refuses new booking requests (I2) and new holds (I4) for any later period.
The calendar (I1) and venue search (J1) show the venue as unavailable from the block's start, with no end, labelled as open-ended.
issues.description:
Ref/ID: I5  
Component/Category: Venue Availability Calendar  
⚠ **NEW — Week 9 answers (W9-FX-3) and decision D-01**, `documentation/clarifications.md`

**Change:** a new requirement on a Done story (course guide, scenario 2). I2 (SPM-35) stays Done; this story replaces I2's "end date/time … mandatory".

**User Story:** As a Venue Staff member, I want to record unavailability without knowing when it will end, so that a venue stays blocked until the problem is fixed.

**Acceptance Criteria**

* A block may be created with no end date and time; it stays active until Venue Staff remove it (I2). When an end is given, it must still be later than the start, as in I2.
* An open-ended block disrupts and flags, as in I2, every confirmed booking, pending request and hold at the venue whose occupied period ends after the block starts.
* From its start, an open-ended block refuses new booking requests (I2) and new holds (I4) for any later period.
* The calendar (I1) and venue search (J1) show the venue as unavailable from the block's start, with no end, labelled as open-ended.

**Source:** "Venue Staff can set temporary unavailability with end dates or leave it open-ended until operational issues are resolved and lifted" (W9-49). This conflicts with W9-41 ("It should not be open-ended"); by D-01 the later answer, W9-49, counts.

**Design and tests to update:** data model (nullable block end), overlap queries, API and OpenAPI for blocks, calendar and search display; regression tests on I2, I1 and J1.

Story points: to be set at planning poker.

To Do

1. Backend: optional end-date migration; open-ended overlap handling.
2. Frontend: until-further-notice option; calendar/search labels.
3. Tests: all four criteria, including bookings months later.
